newsitem.title: JAPAN: Dowa says no word yet on zinc expansion.
newsitem.headline: Dowa says no word yet on zinc expansion.

text.p: Dowa Mining Co and its partners in the Iijima zinc smelter, Japan's largest, have not yet decided on a proposal to boost the plant's output, a Dowa spokeswoman said.

She denied a Japanese trade press report earlier this week that Iijima's owners agreed to raise output by a modest 20,000 tonnes per year to 176,000 tonnes and would implement the expansion when demand conditions were right.
"We're still studying it. It has not been decided yet," the spokeswoman said. She said it may take another two to three months or more before a decision is reached.
She also did not rule out the possibility that the expansion, if approved, could be implemented before the end of this year.

Dowa, which owns a majority stake in the smelter, has reportedly been mulling a 20,000-tonne expansion since the spring of last year. A Dowa executive said last fall that a decision was expected by the end of 1996.

Two Japanese zinc smelters were shuttered in 1995 and 1996, as the yen's sharp rise through the spring of 1995 seriously eroded profits. The treatment charges that smelters receive from mining companies are denominated in dollars, so any rise in the yen directly reduces Japanese smelters' bottom lines.

The yen has steadily weakened in the past 18 months, however, spurring a recovery in smelters' profits. Domestic demand for zinc has also been robust in recent months in the auto industry, a leading zinc consumer.

In a separate move, a source at Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co said the company's majority-owned Hachinohe zinc smelter planned to cut output by 5,000 tonnes in the April-September period of this year due to repairs and maintenance.
Zinc smelters' output plans for this year are currently under close scrutiny as talks continue between miners and smelters to set treatment charges for 1997.

A decision on benchmark charges is expected at an industry conference in California early next month. Miners are bargaining hard for a sharp cut from last year's levels, arguing that ore concentrate supplies have become tight.
